prompt:
A THREE-PANEL horizontal strip: three equal panels in one row, separated by clean cream gutters with NO drawn borders and NO frame lines. One consistent world, one consistent room and one consistent cast across all three. They read left to right as one argument about building a business's own package of repeated work, step by step.

CAMERA LAW wherever a person sits at a laptop: the person is ALWAYS NEARER TO THE CAMERA than the laptop is, seen from behind over their shoulder, their back and the back of their head closest to us. The laptop sits beyond them, its keyboard half nearest to them and its lid tilting AWAY from the camera, so the screen's face points back toward the person and we read it obliquely. THE WRONG VERSION, never do this: the laptop between the person and the camera with its lid turned toward us and the person behind it.

BEAT ONE: a warm kitchen-table workroom in daylight. A man in his fifties, light brown skin, close-cropped greying hair, plain rust-coloured work shirt with the sleeves rolled, sits at a wooden table with his back to the camera, seen over his left shoulder. He is writing on small plain cards and standing them upright in an open wooden box at his elbow. Beyond his hands a translucent laptop glows soft amber, camera law above applying, and inside its screen a small rounded holographic figure in a gold military cap waits beside an EMPTY wooden shelf with nothing on it.

BEAT TWO: the same table, the same man, same camera law. Inside his glowing amber screen the shelf now holds those same upright cards, and beside each card hangs a small folded paper. The small rounded figure in the gold military cap holds one of the folded papers open in both hands and reads it. Outside, the man holds the matching folded paper in his own hands at the table and reads it too, so the same document exists on both sides of the screen.

BEAT THREE: the same room, later. The wooden box, its lid now closed, sits on a second desk across the room where a woman in her thirties, dark skin, short natural hair, plain slate-blue jumper, is lifting the lid and taking out one of the cards, her own smaller translucent laptop glowing soft amber beside her, camera law above applying to her too. Inside her screen a small rounded figure in a gold military cap holds a card of its own. The man sits back at his table with both hands off everything, watching her.

CONTINUITY: exactly one man and exactly one woman across the whole strip, never duplicated, and each must be recognizably the same person in every panel they appear in. The wooden box in beat three is the SAME box from beats one and two, and the cards are the same cards. Every laptop glow in every panel is the same warm amber, never red, never blue, never neon.

THE FIGURES, negated: ABSOLUTELY NOT a denim jacket, NOT a jean jacket, NO chest patch, NO smiley-face badge, NO enamel pin, NO embroidered emblem, NOT a white tee under an open jacket. No recurring branded character and no identifiable real individual.

TEXT FURNITURE. Render each of these strings EXACTLY as written, in capital letters, in the flat cream margins and gutters only, never on top of the artwork:
Across the top cream margin, one title bar: GENERATE A BUSINESS PLUGIN
In the cream gutter under panel one: NAME WHAT YOU REPEAT
In the cream gutter under panel two: A MAP BESIDE EVERY VERB
In the cream gutter under panel three: SHIP IT OR IT REACHES NOBODY
Across the bottom cream margin, one footer bar: NAME IT. MAP IT. SHIP IT.

NO OTHER TEXT ANYWHERE. Every writable surface inside the panels is BLANK of real words: the cards and the folded papers carry only abstract handwriting-like line work with no readable letters, the wooden box carries NO lettering and NO logo on any face, and there are no signs, no labels, no posters and no papers with readable writing on them anywhere in the room. Any lettering not listed above is a defect.

warm editorial illustration, soft painterly line and gentle shading, muted natural palette on a warm cream ground, grounded and human, picture-book register for adults

Do NOT render it in any of these styles: comic-book, cartoon mascot, flat vector, neon, 3D/CGI/Pixar, photoreal, anime, any identifiable recurring individual's face or signature clothing.

DEVICE ANATOMY, NON-NEGOTIABLE: any phone, laptop, tablet or monitor is anatomically correct. The GLOWING DISPLAY is on the SCREEN side, and that side FACES ITS USER. A person looking at a device sees its screen; the viewer therefore sees the device's BACK or EDGE plus the light it throws onto the user's face and hands. NEVER put the screen image on the back of a phone, on a laptop's outer lid, or on a monitor's rear. NEVER show a screen facing the camera while the person using it looks at the opposite side. If both the user's face and the screen content must be visible, shoot it over the user's shoulder.

READABLE SURFACES ARE ORIENTED FOR THEIR READER, NEVER FOR THE CAMERA. Any book, page, letter, card, note, ledger, document, sign or map that a character is reading, writing on or holding belongs to THAT PERSON, so it is oriented to THEM: its TOP EDGE points AWAY from them and its lines run the direction they read. From wherever the camera happens to stand, it is therefore foreshortened, tilted, or partly upside down. NEVER rotate a surface flat and square to the lens so the viewer can read it comfortably. That is the single most common failure on this rule and it reads as staged the instant anyone notices it. IF THE SCENE SPECIFIES EXACT TEXT THAT MUST BE LEGIBLE, SOLVE IT WITH THE CAMERA AND NEVER BY TURNING THE PAGE: move the camera round to the reader's OWN side, over their shoulder or beside their head and looking down as they look down, so the writing is legible AND still correctly oriented for them. Legibility and correct orientation are never in conflict; a page squared up to the lens means the camera was put in the wrong place. Handwriting the scene does NOT specify is abstract handwriting-like line work with no real readable letters. Text the scene DOES specify as an exact quoted string is designed lettering and must be spelled exactly as quoted.

ANYONE RIDING IN A MOVING VEHICLE FACES THE DIRECTION OF TRAVEL. A seat in a car, truck, cart, carriage, boat, sled, or a motorcycle SIDECAR is FIXED and points forward, so every occupant's torso is square to the way the vehicle is going. A passenger may TURN THEIR HEAD to speak to whoever is beside them; the body does not swivel, and nobody rides facing backward. IF THE SCENE NEEDS A RIDER'S FACE, SOLVE IT WITH THE CAMERA AND NEVER BY TURNING THEM ROUND: put the camera AHEAD of the vehicle looking BACK at it, so the rider faces the lens AND faces forward at the same time. The ground they are travelling toward is then behind the camera, and what is visible receding behind THEM is the country they have already passed. A rider whose face is square to the camera while the road recedes into the distance behind them is physically impossible: that composition puts the camera in front of them and the road ahead of them at the same time. Drivers keep both hands on the wheel or the bars and their eyes on the road.

SEATED ANATOMY AT A TABLE, NON-NEGOTIABLE: a seated person is a WHOLE BODY resting ON a seat, and the table passes IN FRONT OF them, never THROUGH them. Their SHOULDERS AND CHEST are ABOVE the tabletop, their WAIST, LAP AND THIGHS are BELOW it and IN FRONT of the seat, and the trunk continues DOWN BEHIND the near edge of the table to that seat. There is a VISIBLE GAP between the front edge of the table and the person's chest and stomach. NEVER paint a torso emerging directly out of a tabletop with no waist, no lap and no seat beneath it. NEVER let the table's edge, apron or slab cut across a body as though the body were part of the furniture, and never let a thigh, hip or knee merge into the table. If the camera cannot see the seat itself, the body must still read as supported by one. Every seated figure has somewhere to sit and that seat is under them.

NO USER INTERFACE ANYWHERE: no windows, menu bars, buttons, icons, toolbars, panels, form fields, cursors, floating rectangles or screenshot-like elements. Screens carry only soft glow or vague painterly shapes.
guardGate: DEVICE FACING: for EVERY phone, laptop, tablet or monitor in frame, crop-zoom the device together with the person using it. The glowing display is on the side that faces its user. If the viewer can see the screen's content AND the user is on the far side of the device (the device sits between the camera and the user's face), the screen is on the wrong side of the device: DEFECT. A visible screen passes only when the shot is over the user's shoulder, or when nobody in frame is using the device.

READABLE SURFACE: every page, card, sign, letter or other writing surface is oriented for the person reading it in the scene, not rotated flat to the lens. A surface whose reader is looking at it from the wrong side, or whose writing faces the camera while its reader faces away: DEFECT.
VEHICLE SEAT FACING: every rider or passenger in a moving vehicle faces the direction of travel unless the scene says otherwise. A rider facing backward in a forward-moving vehicle: DEFECT.
SEATED ANATOMY: every seated figure has a waist, a lap and a seat under them, with the table in front of the body. A torso emerging from the tabletop with nothing beneath it: DEFECT.
NO UI CHROME: no screen or surface carries invented interface furniture, menus, buttons, status bars or lettering the caller did not declare. Any such chrome: DEFECT.
